title: The Mystery of the Dodging Metal
markdown:
“Oh, bother and bits,” Sana said, holding a bent wrench that seemed determined to fly away from Teacher Jae’s giant magnet. They were in the Scrapyard, a maze of rusting metal and rumbling cranes. Today’s challenge: retrieve a crucial metallic component from the centre, guarded by a strange unseen pull.

“It’s not just the wrench,” Tern squawked, circling. “My shiny foil is doing the flutter-shy dance too.” Tern, a gull with a grand ego, loved anything that glinted. His treasures were actively dodging. Their metal tools were supposed to be attracted to Jae’s electromagnets. Instead they were pushed away. Inconvenient, since the target was metallic. The air thrummed with resistance, a low argument you felt in your teeth.

Sana sighed. “Jae said the magnets would help. This feels different. As if the metal is actively dodging.” She kicked a coil of coppery wire. As it brushed a quiet humming generator, a nearby pile of nuts and bolts leapt and skittered, clinging to the wire as if it had become a magnet overnight. A crackle. Rough metal on copper. A faint ozone tickle. The tiny metal army marched onto the wire.

Tern swooped. “Whoa. It’s gobbling the metal.” He nudged the coil. More bits stuck fast. Sana’s tummy did a flip. Generator. Wire. Clinging junk. Jae had talked about things becoming temporarily magnetic.

“Tern.” A grin. “That’s when it clicked.” She connected the wire’s loose ends to the generator’s terminals, careful of the hum. The soft note grew louder, a promising melody. Not hidden treasure. A circuit.

With purpose they approached the yard’s centre. Sana held the now-energised coil. She extended it toward the component. Instead of pushing it away, the wire, alive with current, began to pull. The piece lifted slightly, hovering just above the dirt. “It’s working,” Tern chirped, a victory wobble that nearly cost him a foil sweet. Sana guided the floating component toward them, generator hum as soundtrack. Other students watched as they walked the repulsion the wrong way round.

Back in the classroom Jae smiled. “A puzzle.”

Sana nodded. “The yard pushed us away until the wire suddenly wanted to grab things.”

“Electromagnetism. Current through a wire makes a field. You turned the coil into a temporary magnet.”

Tern tilted his head. “So not sticky wire?”

“Not sticky. Current on, magnet. Current off, just copper.” Jae did not call it a wonderful dance of unseen wonders. They coiled the lead neatly and labelled the terminals so the next group would not lick them, which Tern looked as if he had considered.

Sana looked at the coil, then the yard through the window. She did not inventory invisible forces. She sketched the circuit in her app — generator, coil, pull — and let Tern keep one bolt that had volunteered as a passenger, on the condition it was not a deer, a joke only she found funny, and only a little.
